1.pericope_label: Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man: preserve me from the violent man... O God the Lord, the strength of my salvation, thou hast covered my head in the day of battle

schools.summary: Delitzsch dates the psalm from Absalom's rebellion and grants that its form is more bold than beautiful; Ellicott refuses the singular enemy, re-derives the verb of gathering, and supplies the natural history of the adders.
Gill collects the Jewish attributions and the serpent lore; Calvin rejects the usual identification with Doeg and defends the psalm's temper as a plea of innocence rather than personal abuse.
Clarke names Saul throughout and reads the snares as the machinery of a state prosecution; Wesley glosses the serpent's tongue.
Henry paints the enemies as the seed of the serpent and observes that great persecutors have often been great politicians; Spurgeon makes the plea one against a species rather than a man.
Augustine hears the voice of the Church set among the wicked, and reads the deliverance as sought from the whole class of evil men and from their prince.

debates.question: Who is the evil and violent man?

positions.summary: Saul, and the counsellors who inflamed him — not Doeg, as the great body of interpreters hold, since the context is against it.
Saul, the psalm belonging to the moment when he tried to transfix David with his spear.
Saul as ring-leader, though the Chaldee names both Doeg and Ahithophel despite the distance of time between them.
Not one man at all: the singular must not mislead, since it is immediately changed to the plural.
The situation is that of Absalom's rebellion, with the Benjamite Sheba's attached to it as an outbreak of Ephraimitish jealousy.

debates.question: What are the enemies doing in the second verse?

positions.summary: Continually stirring up wars, the verb better derived from a root meaning to incite than rendered 'gathered together' or 'dwell with wars'.
Plotting secretly and continually, traducing David to Saul and devising means to take his life.

debates.question: How is the imprecatory temper of the psalm to be defended?

positions.summary: David is not multiplying terms of reproach as men do in personal disputes but conciliating God's favour by proving his innocence.
The form is more bold than beautiful, and the language becomes fearfully obscure just where it turns against the enemies.
The plea is against a species rather than a person, and reads like a clause of the Lord's prayer.

outliers.summary: Observes that great persecutors have often been great politicians, which has made them the more formidable — but that the Lord preserves the simple without any of those arts.

Supplies the zoology of the adders: the Hebrew word occurs only here and has been explained as a compound meaning that which rolls itself up and lies in ambush, with a naturalist's report of the vipers common in Syria.

themes: Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man: preserve me from the violent man;
Which imagine mischiefs in their heart; continually are they gathered together for war.
They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; adders’ poison is under their lips. Selah.
Keep me, O Lord, from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from the violent man; who have purposed to overthrow my goings.
The proud have hid a snare for me, and cords; they have spread a net by the wayside; they have set gins for me. Selah.
I said unto the Lord, Thou art my God: hear the voice of my supplications, O Lord.
O God the Lord, the strength of my salvation, thou hast covered my head in the day of battle.

8.pericope_label: Grant not, O Lord, the desires of the wicked: further not his wicked device... Surely the righteous shall give thanks unto thy name: the upright shall dwell in thy presence

schools.summary: Ellicott treats the closing verses as a damaged text and proposes a series of emendations; Delitzsch marks the change of mood at the end and generalises the promise to the whole good cause.
Gill reads the coals of both this life and hell, identifies the man of tongue, and notes the double reading at the twelfth verse.
Clarke draws a doctrine of the resurrection out of the Chaldee's paraphrase and expounds the three-forked tongue; Wesley reduces the coals to divine vengeance.
Henry reads the eighth verse as a prayer for disappointment rather than destruction; Spurgeon relishes the retaliation and calls the psalm grandly positive.

debates.question: Is the eighth verse a prayer or a prophecy?

positions.summary: A prayer for disappointment rather than destruction — that providence should not favour their designs — though some choose to read it as prophecy.
A prayer that God may disappoint and confound enemies still plotting his death.
A deprecation grounded on the fact that the desires of the wicked are under God's restraint and cannot be fulfilled without his leave.

debates.question: Is the text of the closing imprecations sound?

positions.summary: No: the versions insert a negative and take a noun as a verb, the word lift up belongs to the following verse, a clause has probably dropped out, and the tenth verse needs a further change to give a grammatical sentence.
Read as it stands, of coals falling from heaven as at Sodom, covering the judgments of this life and everlasting burnings.

debates.question: What is the man of tongue?

positions.summary: A man of detraction with a three-forked tongue, wounding three at once — the neighbour he slanders, the one who receives it, and himself who deals in it.
One who sets his mouth against the heavens and whose tongue walks through the earth.
Literally a man of tongue, and probably some particular person noted for the violence of his speech.

outliers.summary: Argues from the Chaldee's paraphrase — miry pits from which they shall have no resurrection to eternal life — that the Jews did believe in a resurrection of the body.
Marks the change of key at the close: the rage having spent itself, the mood and language become cheerful and the psalm trips along merrily to the end.

themes: Grant not, O Lord, the desires of the wicked: further not his wicked device; lest they exalt themselves. Selah.
As for the head of those that compass me about, let the mischief of their own lips cover them.
Let burning coals fall upon them: let them be cast into the fire; into deep pits, that they rise not up again.
Let not an evil speaker be established in the earth: evil shall hunt the violent man to overthrow him.
I know that the Lord will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and the right of the poor.
Surely the righteous shall give thanks unto thy name: the upright shall dwell in thy presence.
